summary: The Internet Printing Protocol is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This document, on the standards track as an internet standard, defines how IPP operations, attributes and values are encoded into the application/ipp media type and how those messages are carried over HTTP.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) lets clients send operations to printers over a network. RFC 8010 defines the structure of those messages and how HTTP carries them.

questions: how does ipp work over http
what is the internet printing protocol
what is the difference between ipp and ipps
subtitle: How IPP operations are encoded as bytes and carried in HTTP messages.

tldr.problem: A print client and a printer need to agree on how operations, attributes, and document data are encoded and transported.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8010 defines the application/ipp message format and rules for carrying it in HTTP requests and responses, including use of POST and the default port 631.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2910 and RFC 3382. The operation meanings are defined in the companion Model and Semantics document, RFC 8011.

today: RFC 8010 is an Internet Standard published in January 2017. It obsoletes RFC 2910 and RFC 3382; read it with RFC 8011 for operation meanings.

sections.title: The Operation and Transport Layers
sections.content:
IPP has an operation layer and a transport layer. The operation layer is the message body that describes a request or response. The transport layer is an HTTP request and response carrying that body.

RFC 8010 specifies the operation encoding and HTTP transport rules. The meanings of operations, attributes, and values are in the IPP Model and Semantics document, RFC 8011. HTTP/1.1 is required; HTTP/2 is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPP message has a body containing the print operation, carried inside an HTTP exchange. This RFC defines the message structure and transport rules.

sections.title: The IPP Message Layout
sections.content:
An IPP request or response begins with a two-byte version number, a two-byte operation identifier or status code, and a four-byte request identifier. It then contains zero or more attribute groups, a required end-of-attributes tag, and optional document data.

Each attribute group starts with a delimiter tag. The end-of-attributes tag has value 0x03 and must appear exactly once. If the message includes document data, that data follows the tag. The IPP/1.1 version is encoded as major and minor values of 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPP message begins with its version, operation or status, and request identifier. Attribute groups follow, then a marker ends the attributes before any document data.

sections.title: Encoding Attributes and Values
sections.content:
An attribute value begins with a one-byte value tag that identifies its type, followed by the name length, name, value length, and value. Lengths count octets. A further value for the same attribute has a zero-length name, which is the encoding's way to mark an additional value.

Integers use signed two's-complement values in big-endian order. Integer and enumeration values use four octets; booleans use one octet. A collection begins with the begCollection tag, contains member attributes, and ends with the endCollection tag.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute states what type of value follows and how long its name and value are. Repeated values use a zero-length name to show they belong to the same attribute.

sections.title: Carrying IPP Over HTTP
sections.content:
Each IPP operation uses an HTTP POST request, with application/ipp as the Content-Type in requests and responses. Printers must support HTTP over the assigned default port 631 and may support other ports. HTTP/1.1 servers must support chunked IPP requests, and clients must support chunked IPP responses.

The target is identified both in the HTTP request and in an operation attribute such as printer-uri or job-uri. The two identifiers may have different forms, but they must refer to the same object. The URI inside the IPP operation attribute must be absolute.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends each IPP operation in an HTTP POST request. It names the target in both HTTP and the IPP body, and both names must identify the same printer or job.

sections.title: IPP and IPPS Addresses
sections.content:
IPP uses ipp URIs, and secure IPP uses ipps URIs. For the HTTP layer, a client changes ipp to http or ipps to https and adds port 631 when the URI has no explicit port. The original ipp or ipps URI remains in the IPP message body.

For an ipp URI, HTTP can request an upgrade to TLS. For an ipps URI, the client and server negotiate TLS immediately. The RFC recommends TLS support because print jobs can contain sensitive information; it also describes authentication requirements and certificate handling.
sections.plainLanguage: The client changes an ipp address to an HTTP address for transport, while keeping the original IPP address in the message body. The ipps scheme starts a secure TLS connection.
